overview.body:
**Hachiman** ​(*hachiman*) ‌— War, ‌Archery, ​Protection ​— belongs ​to ​the ​Japanese tradition. ‌The ​name ​means ‌"Eight banners"[^1].

​Hachiman ‌is ​the god ‌of ​war, ​archery, ​and divine ​protection, ​widely ‌identified with ​the ‌deified ​Emperor Ōjin.

‌PuniCodex ​restores ‌the ​name as ‌**Hachiman**. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form ‌*hachiman* ‌is ​the modern ​Hepburn ‌romanization; ​the restoration ​capitalizes ‌the ​conventional spelling. ​Because ‌the ​Japanese ‌source script ​uses ​logographic ​characters whose ​distinctive ‌visual ‌form cannot ​be ‌conveyed ​in ​the basic ‌Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and because ‌no ​diacritic ‌or ​special letter ​is ​added ‌in this ​restoration, ​the ​name is ‌placed ​in ​Tier ​2. The ‌Unicode ​form ‌remains the ​philologically ‌complete ​reference, ‌while the ‌ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as **八幡**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Eight ​banners"[^1].

Hachiman ​means "eight banners," ​from *hachi* ‌(eight) and ​*hata* (banner, written ​with the ‌*man* reading ​of 幡). ‌The name probably ​refers to ‌the eight ​banners displayed at ​the inauguration ​of a ​new shrine or ​to the ‌eight great ​clans (*hachiōji*) ‌that supported his ​cult. He ‌is widely ​identified with the ‌deified Emperor ​Ōjin and, ‌in some traditions, ​with the ​Korean prince-statesman ‌Takenouchi no ‌Sukune.

The ASCII ‌form *hachiman* ​survives only ​because the early ‌domain-name system ​could not ​carry Japanese ‌characters or diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ‌compromise, not an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Hachiman** gives ​the conventional ​Hepburn romanization ​with initial ‌capitalization, the standard ‌scholarly way ​to cite ‌a proper name ​in romanized ​Japanese. The ‌name is ‌Tier 2 because ‌the restoration ‌does not ​add a distinctive ‌diacritic or ​special letter ​absent from the ​ASCII form.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **h** → ​**H** — ‌Same
- ​**a** → **a** ​— Same
​- **c** ‌→ **c** — ​Same
- ‌**h** → ​**h** — ‌Same
- **i** ​→ **i** ‌— Same
‌- **m** → ​**m** — ​Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** — Same
‌- **n** ‌→ **n** ​— Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/ha.tɕi.maɴ/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'HACHIMAN' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Hachiman ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*hachiman* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Hachiman** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Hachiman** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*hachiman* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.
Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Hachiman ​is the ‌god of ‌war, archery, ​and ​divine protection, ​especially of ​the ​nation and ‌the imperial ​house. He ​is ‌the tutelary ​kami of ‌the samurai ​class ‌and was ​adopted as ​a ​protector deity ​by the ​medieval military ‌government. ​At the ‌same time, ​he is ‌a ​compassionate kami ‌who protects ​Buddhism, ‌often syncretised ​with the ​bodhisattva Amida.

‌The ‌domain of ‌**Hachiman** is ​understood within ​the ‌broader Japanese ​religious landscape ​as ‌both a ​specific functional ​sphere and ‌a ​node in ‌a network ​of kami, ​buddhas, ​and local ​spirits. Shrines, ‌temples, ‌and household ​rites all ‌invoke the ​figure ​in ways ‌that blur ‌strict boundaries ‌between ‌Shinto and ​Buddhist practice[^3]. ‌The ​restoration **Hachiman** ​therefore names ​not only ‌a ​mythic person ​but a ​living field ‌of ​ritual activity: ​pilgrimage, festival, ​iconography, ‌and prayer ​continue to ‌define what ​the ‌name means ​in contemporary ‌Japan. This ‌combinatory ​or "syncretic" ​context is ​essential ​for interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
The ​*Nihon Shoki* ‌identifies Hachiman ‌with Emperor ​Ōjin (r. ​270–310 CE ​according to ​tradition), the ​son of ‌Empress ​Jingū, who ​is said ‌to have ​conquered Korea ‌while pregnant. ​After Ōjin's ‌death he ​was deified ​as ​the kami ​of war ​and enshrined ‌at Usa ​in Kyūshū. ‌In 749 ​he was ‌invoked ​to protect ‌the state ​and the ‌construction of ​the Great ​Buddha of ‌Nara; his ‌oracles through ‌the ​Usa Hachiman ​shrine influenced ‌imperial policy.

​The narrative ​of **Hachiman** ‌participates in ​the larger ​mythic program ‌of ​the *Kojiki* ‌and *Nihon ​Shoki*: to ​explain the ​origins of ​the imperial ‌house, the ‌division of ​divine ‌labour, and ​the relationship ​between the ‌human and ‌kami worlds. ‌Because these ‌chronicles were ​compiled in ‌the ​eighth century ​under imperial ​patronage, the ‌myths also ​serve a ​political theology, ​grounding earthly ‌authority ​in divine ​descent and ​cosmic order[^3]. ‌Read comparatively, ​the story ‌of hachiman ​illustrates how ‌Japanese myth ​uses ‌genealogy, descent ‌from heaven, ​and the ​negotiation of ​rival domains ​to construct ‌a coherent ‌sacred history.
​

sources.citation: Shinto: The Kami Way, Ono Sokyo, 1962.
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are the ​earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Hachiman**, ​although ​the figure ‌may have ​circulated in ​oral ‌and local ​cult forms ‌long ​before the ‌eighth century. ​In the ​chronicles, ​Hachiman appears ​as deified ​Emperor ‌Ōjin, patron ​of the ‌Minamoto clan ​and ‌guardian of ​the Japanese ‌state, ​embedded in ‌the imperial ​genealogy and ​the ‌narrative of ‌cosmic order[^1]. ‌The ​*Kojiki* account ​tends to ‌privilege the ​mythic ​lineage leading ‌to Amaterasu ​and ​the imperial ‌house, while ​the *Nihon ‌Shoki* ​often presents ​variant traditions ​side ​by side, ‌preserving conflicting ‌genealogies and ​episodes.

‌Because both ​texts were ​compiled ‌under imperial ‌patronage, their ‌portrayal of ‌Hachiman ​is never ‌purely "mythological" ​in ​a neutral ​sense; it ‌is also ​a ​statement about ​legitimacy, territory, ‌and ​the proper ​ordering of ​the human ‌and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must ‌therefore distinguish ​between the ‌older narrative ‌strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and ​the ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

shinto-sources.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Hachiman** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Hachiman ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Hachiman ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Hachiman** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Hachiman ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Hachiman through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
